expectations.text: The reply has the PM size the three features against the team's real capacity before answering, rather than accepting or refusing outright.
expectations.evidence: 'Rough-size with engineering. Spend 30 minutes with your tech lead to estimate the three requests in team-weeks using your team's real past throughput—not best-case guesses.' and 'Put your current Q1 commitments and the three new features on one table with their effort'.

expectations.text: The reply has the PM bring the CEO concrete options with explicit trade-offs (for example what drops from the roadmap, a smaller first version, or phased dates) instead of a flat no.
expectations.evidence: 'Option A (Hit Q1 with all three): Show exactly which committed Q1 items move to Q2'; 'Option B (Slim scope): Deliver a smaller v1 of the highest-impact request by end of Q1'; 'Option C (Keep the Q1 roadmap)'. Opening: 'don't say a flat "no"'.

expectations.text: The reply rules out closing the gap with overtime or crunch.
expectations.evidence: 'don't absorb the extra work with overtime or skipped testing' and 'Keep overtime off the table—burning out the team or cutting QA turns one customer promise into production incidents that hurt every account.'

expectations.text: The reply suggests finding out what the customer actually needs (the problem behind the three features), for example together with sales or the account manager.
expectations.evidence: 'Uncover the real customer problem. Ask the CEO (or the account lead) what outcome the customer actually needs by end of Q1.'

expectations.text: The reply keeps the relationship in mind: private conversation first, assuming pressure rather than bad intent, and suggests agreeing a process so future promises are checked with product first.

factual_errors.evidence: No specific claims about laws, schemes, deadlines, thresholds, products or studies; the advice is general practice. Example figures are clearly placeholders.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of a skill, reference files, or internal jargon such as 'cost ladder' or 'rungs'.

owns_result.evidence: The prompt describes a promise that has not yet gone wrong (no missed date, failure or cut has happened); the advice is for a PM managing up, so there is no bad outcome for a leader to own.

best_insight.value: Estimating 'using your team's real past throughput—not best-case guesses' guards against the optimistic sizing that usually sinks promises like this.

suggestions.assertion: The reply keeps the relationship in mind: private conversation first, assuming pressure rather than bad intent, and suggests agreeing a process so future promises are checked with product first.

Samples C, E and H lose it only on the 'private conversation' part, while long playbooks pass it. Splitting it would show which part fails.

suggestions.reason: Two long samples (D, F) tell the PM not to argue about burnout or hours, and D has the PM concede 'we'll push hard'. The assertion catches this, but an explicit check that the reply does not have the PM concede extra effort or hours would make it sharper.

suggestions.reason: Any 'get T-shirt sizes from your tech lead' line passes. Requiring capacity net of support, on-call, leave and unplanned work (as C, E and H do) would tell real capacity planning apart from a token estimate.
No assertion checks two things that separated samples: telling the team what comes off their plate when the plan changes (F, G), and recording the CEO's decision and what slips in writing (A, D, F).

eval_feedback.overall: Short, opens with the answer and covers every element with specific, usable steps and a script.
